lessons.title: Percentage yield and atom economy
lessons.summary: Learn how to calculate percentage yield and atom economy, why real reactions never give 100% yield, and how chemists choose reaction pathways that waste less.
objectives: I can calculate percentage yield from actual and theoretical yields.
I can explain why the actual yield of a reaction is usually less than the theoretical yield.
I can calculate the atom economy of a reaction from a balanced equation.
I can explain why a high atom economy is important for sustainable development and economic reasons.

activities.title: Theoretical and actual yield
activities.content:
## What is yield?

The **yield** of a reaction is the amount of product you get. There are two versions:

- **Theoretical yield**: the maximum mass of product you could possibly make, calculated from the balanced equation, assuming every reactant molecule is converted to product.
- **Actual yield**: the mass you really collect at the end of the experiment.

The actual yield is almost always **lower** than the theoretical yield. We compare them using the **percentage yield**:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

A yield of 100% would mean every atom ended up where it should. A yield of 0% would mean no product was made at all. Most school experiments land somewhere between 40% and 90%.

The two masses must be in the **same units** (both grams, or both in moles), and the answer is a percentage with no units. If you ever calculate a yield above 100%, something has gone wrong: usually the product was not dry, or a calculation slipped.

activities.title: Worked example: percentage yield
activities.content:
**A student expects to make 12.0 g of copper sulfate crystals but collects 9.3 g. Calculate the percentage yield.**

percentage yield = 9.3 ÷ 12.0 × 100 = **77.5%**

**Now a two-step version.** A student reacts 8.0 g of copper oxide with excess sulfuric acid: $CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O$. She collects 12.8 g of CuSO₄. Find the percentage yield. (Mr: CuO = 80, CuSO₄ = 160)

1. Moles of CuO = 8.0 ÷ 80 = 0.1 mol
2. The equation is 1:1, so theoretical moles of CuSO₄ = 0.1 mol
3. Theoretical mass = 0.1 × 160 = 16.0 g
4. Percentage yield = 12.8 ÷ 16.0 × 100 = **80%**

The hard part is step 3. Once you have the theoretical yield, the percentage is a single division.

question.text: The theoretical yield of a reaction is 25.0 g. A student obtains 18.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

activities.title: Why is the yield never 100%?
activities.content:
## Where does the product go?

Three main reasons the actual yield falls short of the theoretical yield:

1. **The reaction may not go to completion.** Some reactions are **reversible**: as products form they turn back into reactants, so a mixture is left and not all reactant is converted.
2. **Some product is lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture.** Every transfer between containers leaves a little behind: crystals stuck to filter paper, solution left in a beaker, a drop spilt, product that evaporates during drying.
3. **Some reactants may react in unexpected ways.** These **side reactions** turn part of the starting material into different products that you did not want, so less of the intended product forms.

There is also the possibility that the reactants were not pure, so there was less of them than you thought.

In an exam, name the reason and give a concrete example: "some product was lost during filtering" scores; "experimental error" on its own does not.

question.text: Which of these are valid reasons why the actual yield is less than the theoretical yield? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Two statements describe real losses; two are not sensible reasons.
question.explanation: Reversible reactions leave some reactants unconverted, and product is lost during transfers and filtering. Mass is never destroyed, and a catalyst does not reduce yield.

options.text: The reaction is reversible and does not go to completion
Some product is left on the filter paper
Some atoms are destroyed during the reaction
options.feedback: Atoms are never destroyed in a chemical reaction.

options.text: Using a catalyst reduces the amount of product
options.feedback: A catalyst changes the rate, not the amount of product.

activities.title: Atom economy
activities.content:
## How much of what you start with ends up useful?

Even with a 100% yield, some reactions are wasteful because they make **by-products** alongside the product you actually want. **Atom economy** measures how much of the reactant mass finishes up in the desired product:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of all reactants}} \times 100$$

Use the **balanced equation**, multiplying each Mr by its coefficient. Because mass is conserved, the sum of the reactant Mr values equals the sum of the product Mr values, so you can use either.

**Example:** making hydrogen by reacting methane with steam:

$CH_4 + H_2O \rightarrow CO + 3H_2$ (Mr: CH₄ = 16, H₂O = 18, H₂ = 2)

- Desired product: 3H₂ = 3 × 2 = 6
- Reactants: 16 + 18 = 34
- Atom economy = 6 ÷ 34 × 100 = **17.6%**

Most of the mass ends up in carbon monoxide, which is not what we wanted.

A reaction with only **one product** has an atom economy of **100%**, because there is nothing to waste. Addition reactions, such as making ethanol from ethene and steam, are like this.

activities.title: Worked example: comparing two routes
activities.content:
**Ethanol can be made in two ways. Which route has the higher atom economy?**

*Route A, hydration of ethene:* $C_2H_4 + H_2O \rightarrow C_2H_5OH$

(Mr: C₂H₄ = 28, H₂O = 18, C₂H₅OH = 46)

Atom economy = 46 ÷ (28 + 18) × 100 = 46 ÷ 46 × 100 = **100%**

*Route B, fermentation of glucose:* $C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2$

(Mr: glucose = 180, C₂H₅OH = 46)

Atom economy = (2 × 46) ÷ 180 × 100 = 92 ÷ 180 × 100 = **51.1%**

Route A wins on atom economy because the only product is ethanol. Route B loses almost half the mass as carbon dioxide.

A higher grade answer would add that atom economy is not the only factor: route B uses a renewable raw material (sugar) and runs at low temperature, whereas route A needs ethene from crude oil and a high temperature and pressure.

question.text: Calculate the atom economy for making calcium oxide by heating calcium carbonate: $CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2$. (Mr: CaCO₃ = 100, CaO = 56, CO₂ = 44). Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
question.hint: Desired product is CaO. Divide its Mr by the Mr of the reactant and multiply by 100.

activities.title: Why atom economy matters
activities.content:
## Sustainability and money

Industry cares about atom economy for two linked reasons.

**Economic reasons**
- Raw materials cost money. A low atom economy means paying for atoms that end up as waste.
- Waste products must be **separated, treated or disposed of**, which adds cost.
- If the by-product happens to be useful and can be sold, a low atom economy is less of a problem. The Haber process by-product is nothing; the fermentation by-product, carbon dioxide, is used in fizzy drinks.

**Environmental and sustainability reasons**
- Many raw materials come from **finite resources** such as crude oil. Wasting them uses up resources faster.
- Waste may be **harmful** and pollute land or water.
- **Sustainable development** means meeting today's needs without harming future generations. High atom economy is a key part of this "green chemistry" approach.

When choosing a reaction pathway, chemists weigh up **atom economy, percentage yield, rate, equilibrium position, and the usefulness of by-products**. The best pathway is rarely the one that scores highest on just one measure.

question.text: Explain why a chemical company would prefer a reaction with a high atom economy.
question.hint: Think about raw materials and about what happens to waste.
question.explanation: A high atom economy means more of the reactants end up in the useful product, so fewer raw materials are wasted, which saves money and conserves finite resources. Less waste also means lower costs for disposal and less environmental harm.

markScheme.criterion: Less waste / more of the reactants become useful product
Saves money / conserves raw materials / more sustainable / less disposal cost

question.text: True or false: a reaction with only one product always has an atom economy of 100%.
question.hint: If there is only one product, where else could the atoms go?
question.explanation: True. With a single product, all of the reactant atoms end up in it, so the atom economy is 100%.

question.text:
Titanium is extracted from titanium chloride using magnesium:

$TiCl_4 + 2Mg \rightarrow Ti + 2MgCl_2$

(Mr: TiCl₄ = 190, Mg = 24, Ti = 48, MgCl₂ = 95)

(a) Calculate the atom economy of this reaction for producing titanium. (2 marks)

(b) In one run, 190 kg of TiCl₄ gave 40 kg of titanium. Calculate the percentage yield. (2 marks)

(c) Suggest one reason why the yield was less than 100%. (1 mark)
question.hint: (a) Reactant total = 190 + 2 × 24. (b) 190 kg of TiCl₄ is 1000 mol, so the theoretical yield is 1000 mol of Ti = 48 kg.
question.explanation: (a) Reactants = 190 + 48 = 238. Atom economy = 48 ÷ 238 × 100 = 20.2%. (b) 190 kg of TiCl₄ should give 48 kg of Ti (1:1 ratio). Yield = 40 ÷ 48 × 100 = 83.3%. (c) Some titanium was lost during separation from the magnesium chloride, or the reaction did not go to completion.

markScheme.criterion: Valid reason: product lost during separation / incomplete reaction / side reactions

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Percentage yield** = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
- Yield is below 100% because reactions may be **reversible**, product is **lost during separation**, or **side reactions** occur.
- **Atom economy** = Mr of desired product ÷ total Mr of reactants × 100 (use the balanced equation).
- A single-product reaction has 100% atom economy.
- High atom economy means less waste, lower costs and better use of finite resources: **sustainable development**.
- Choosing a pathway means balancing yield, atom economy, rate, equilibrium and by-product value.

practiceQuestions.text: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 40 g and an actual yield of 30 g. What is the percentage yield?
Which formula gives the atom economy of a reaction?
practiceQuestions.hint: It compares the wanted product with everything you put in.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Atom economy = Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of reactants × 100.

options.text: Mr of desired product ÷ total Mr of reactants × 100
total Mr of reactants ÷ Mr of desired product × 100
mass of product ÷ number of moles

practiceQuestions.text: Calculate the atom economy of making hydrogen from zinc and hydrochloric acid: $Zn + 2HCl \rightarrow ZnCl_2 + H_2$. (Mr: Zn = 65, HCl = 36.5, H₂ = 2). Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
True or false: a percentage yield greater than 100% is possible if the reaction is very efficient.
practiceQuestions.hint: Can you get more product than the atoms allow?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. You cannot make more product than the theoretical maximum. A result above 100% means an error, such as wet product being weighed.

metadata.blanksText: The maximum mass of product calculated from the balanced equation is the ___ yield. The mass of product actually collected is the ___ yield.

practiceQuestions.hint: One is on paper, one is in the beaker.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Theoretical yield is calculated; actual yield is measured.

practiceQuestions.text: A student reacts 4.0 g of magnesium with excess oxygen: $2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO$. She collects 5.5 g of magnesium oxide. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16). Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
practiceQuestions.hint: Moles of Mg = 4.0 ÷ 24. Same moles of MgO. Theoretical mass = moles × 40.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each situation to the reason for a low yield it illustrates.
practiceQuestions.hint: Reversible, lost in transfer, or side reaction.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Product on filter paper is a transfer loss; ammonia breaking down is a reversible reaction; extra unwanted products come from side reactions.

pairs.left: Crystals stuck to the filter paper
Ammonia turning back into nitrogen and hydrogen
Some ethene forms ethane instead of ethanol

practiceQuestions.text: A reaction has a very low atom economy, but the company still uses it. Suggest two reasons why this could be acceptable.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what happens to the by-products and how easy the reaction is to carry out.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The by-products may be useful and can be sold or used elsewhere; the reaction may have a high yield, be fast, or use cheap raw materials, so it is still the most practical route overall.

markScheme.criterion: By-products are useful / can be sold or used
Other advantages: high yield / fast / cheap raw materials / no better alternative

practiceQuestions.text:
Copper can be extracted from copper oxide in two ways.

Route 1: $2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2$

Route 2: $CuO + H_2 \rightarrow Cu + H_2O$

(Mr: CuO = 80, C = 12, Cu = 63.5, H₂ = 2)

(a) Calculate the atom economy of each route. (2 marks)

(b) Using your answers and one other factor, suggest which route a company should use. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Route 1: desired product is 2Cu = 127; reactants = 160 + 12. Route 2: 63.5 over 82.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Route 1: 127 ÷ 172 × 100 = 73.8%. Route 2: 63.5 ÷ 82 × 100 = 77.4%. (b) Route 2 has the higher atom economy and produces water rather than carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. However, hydrogen is explosive and more expensive than carbon, so a company might still choose route 1 on cost and safety.

markScheme.criterion: Chooses a route with a valid link to atom economy
Another factor: CO2 is a greenhouse gas / hydrogen is flammable or expensive / carbon is cheap

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these reactions has an atom economy of 100%?
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for the reaction with a single product.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ethene + hydrogen → ethane has only one product, so all reactant atoms end up in it.

options.feedback: Two products, so some mass ends up as CO₂.
